gloss: The back part of something.
examples: The kitchen is at the *rear* of the house.
Two officers rode at the *rear* of the column.
We parked around the *rear* of the building.

gloss: A period in which something becomes strong or active again after a decline.
examples: The downtown is going through a *rebirth*.
The album marked the band's *rebirth*.
Spring felt like a *rebirth* after that long winter.

gloss: A sharp expression of disapproval.
examples: The senator issued a public *rebuke* of the decision.
Her only *rebuke* was a long silence.
The ruling was a stinging *rebuke* to the agency.

gloss: An argument made to show that something said earlier is wrong.
examples: The defense gave a point-by-point *rebuttal*.
His *rebuttal* took up the whole second page.
Both *rebuttals* missed the main issue.

gloss: A container or wall fitting that something is put into.
examples: Please drop your cups in the *receptacle* by the door.
The electrician added two *receptacles* to the back wall.
Every *receptacle* in the lab was labeled.

gloss: A part of a cell or nerve that reacts to light, chemicals, or other signals.
examples: The drug blocks a *receptor* in the brain.
Pain *receptors* in the skin fire almost instantly.
Each *receptor* responds to one kind of molecule.

gloss: An arrangement in which two sides give each other equal treatment or benefits.
examples: The two states have *reciprocity* on teaching licenses.
The deal rests on *reciprocity*, not charity.
There was no *reciprocity* in that friendship at all.

gloss: The act of saying something aloud from memory, or a listing of facts one after another.
examples: The class ended with a *recitation* of the poem.
His answer was a dull *recitation* of dates.
We sat through two *recitations* before lunch.

gloss: A complete lack of care about danger or consequences.
examples: The jury found *recklessness*, not intent.
His *recklessness* behind the wheel cost him his license.
There is a line between courage and *recklessness*.

gloss: A time when someone must face the results of past actions, or a calculation of an amount.
examples: The industry is facing a *reckoning* over safety.
By my *reckoning*, we need three more chairs.
A day of *reckoning* was coming for the mayor.

gloss: The process of making damaged or unusable land or material fit for use again.
examples: The city funded a wetland *reclamation* project.
Water *reclamation* keeps the golf courses green.
*Reclamation* of the old mine will take a decade.

gloss: The act of knowing someone or something from before, or public credit for what someone has done.
examples: She got an award in *recognition* of her research.
There was no flicker of *recognition* on his face.
Voice *recognition* still struggles with strong accents.

gloss: A machine that records sound or data, or a simple woodwind instrument played in schools.
examples: The flight *recorder* was found two miles away.
Every third grader here learns the *recorder*.
He kept a small *recorder* in his coat pocket.

gloss: A second count of votes made to check the first result.
examples: The candidate demanded a *recount*.
The *recount* changed the margin by twelve votes.
Two *recounts* confirmed the same winner.
contrast: The noun is REE-kownt; the verb *recount* (to tell a story) is rih-KOWNT, stressed on the second syllable.

gloss: A way of getting help or justice when something goes wrong.
examples: Tenants have legal *recourse* if the heat fails.
She had no *recourse* but to sue.
Without a receipt you have little *recourse*.

gloss: The last section of the large intestine, ending at the anus.
examples: The exam checks the *rectum* for polyps.
Bleeding from the *rectum* should be reported to a doctor.
The surgeon removed a growth in the *rectum*.
contrast: The everyday plural is *rectums*; the Latin *recta* shows up only in medical writing.

gloss: Another occurrence of something that happened before, especially an illness.
examples: She has been free of *recurrence* for five years.
The report warns of a *recurrence* of flooding.
Two *recurrences* in one winter is unusual.

gloss: The act of being freed from blame or sin, or of making up for a past wrong.
examples: The movie is a story of crime and *redemption*.
He saw the job as a shot at *redemption*.
There is no *redemption* without honesty.

gloss: An insulting American label for a poor, rural, conservative white person.
examples: He was tired of being called a *redneck* for his accent.
The show leans on tired jokes about *rednecks*.
Some people use *redneck* about themselves with pride.
contrast: This is an insult in most mouths — use it only when quoting someone, not to describe a person.

gloss: Payment or action that makes up for a wrong someone has suffered.
examples: The families are seeking *redress* in federal court.
The law offers little *redress* for losses like these.
They asked the school for *redress* after the injury.

gloss: A decrease in the size, amount, or price of something.
examples: The plan calls for a ten percent *reduction* in staff.
We saw a big *reduction* in noise after the fence went up.
Both *reductions* take effect in January.

gloss: Extra capacity or repetition built in so that one failure does not stop everything.
examples: The data center has *redundancy* in every power line.
The edit cut a lot of *redundancy* out of the draft.
We build *redundancies* into the schedule.
contrast: In British English *redundancy* also means losing a job; Americans say *layoff* for that.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A very tall evergreen tree of the California coast, or the reddish wood it gives.
examples: The *redwoods* along that highway are two thousand years old.
He built the deck out of *redwood*.
A single *redwood* can top three hundred feet.

gloss: A tall grass that grows in wet ground, or the thin vibrating strip in a woodwind instrument.
examples: Ducks nested among the *reeds* at the edge of the pond.
He soaked a new *reed* before the concert.
The *reed* on my clarinet cracked.
contrast: *Reed* sounds exactly like *read* in the past tense: "I read it yesterday."

gloss: The act of being voted into the same office again.
examples: The governor is running for *reelection*.
His *reelection* was never in doubt.
She lost her bid for *reelection* by four points.
contrast: Often written with a hyphen, *re-election*; both spellings are standard in the US.

gloss: A performance that acts out a past event again.
examples: We watched a Civil War *reenactment* in the park.
Police staged a *reenactment* of the crash.
The museum holds *reenactments* every summer.

gloss: The act of entering something again, such as a spacecraft returning through the atmosphere or a person returning to ordinary life.
examples: The capsule glowed bright during *reentry*.
The program helps with *reentry* after prison.
Two *reentries* were scrubbed for weather.

gloss: A mention of something, a source pointed to for information, or a statement about someone from a former employer.
examples: The article makes no *reference* to the earlier study.
Please list three *references* on the application.
Keep the manual for *reference*.

gloss: A small improvement that makes something better, or elegance of taste and manners.
examples: The new model adds a few *refinements* to the engine.
Her writing has a *refinement* the early drafts lacked.
One more *refinement* and the design is done.

gloss: An automatic movement the body makes without any thought.
examples: The doctor tapped my knee to test the *reflex*.
Goalies need very fast *reflexes*.
Blinking is a *reflex*, not a choice.

gloss: Someone who works to change a system or institution for the better.
examples: She was a tireless *reformer* of the prison system.
*Reformers* pushed the bill through in one session.
The party's *reformers* lost the vote.

gloss: A line or group of lines repeated in a song or poem, or a phrase someone keeps saying.
examples: Everyone sang along on the *refrain*.
"Not my job" became his standard *refrain*.
The two *refrains* use the same melody.

gloss: A short course or reminder that brings back knowledge someone already had.
examples: The nurses take a CPR *refresher* every year.
Give me a quick *refresher* on the rules.
Both *refreshers* are online now.

gloss: An act of saying no to something offered or demanded.
examples: His *refusal* to sign held up the whole deal.
We got a flat *refusal* from the bank.
Two *refusals* in a row ended the negotiation.

gloss: Respect or careful attention given to someone or something.
examples: She is held in high *regard* by her colleagues.
He drove with no *regard* for the speed limit.
With *regard* to your question, the answer is yes.

gloss: A style of popular music from Jamaica with a strong offbeat rhythm.
examples: The bar plays *reggae* every Thursday night.
He grew up on *reggae* and soul.
*Reggae* went worldwide in the 1970s.

gloss: A planned routine of treatment, exercise, or diet.
examples: The doctor put him on a new drug *regimen*.
Her training *regimen* starts at five in the morning.
Both *regimens* gave similar results.
contrast: Do not mix up *regimen* (a routine), *regiment* (an army unit), and *regime* (a government).

gloss: An official who keeps records, especially of students at a college or of births and deaths.
examples: Send the transcript request to the *registrar*.
The county *registrar* certified the results.
Two *registrars* handle all the paperwork.

gloss: A return to an earlier or worse condition, or a statistical method for finding relationships in data.
examples: The tantrums were a *regression* to toddler behavior.
They ran a *regression* on twenty years of data.
Sleep *regressions* are common at eight months.

gloss: The quality of happening at even, predictable intervals.
examples: The trains run with clockwork *regularity*.
He calls his mother with real *regularity*.
The *regularity* of her habits surprised us.

gloss: Something presented again with only small changes and nothing new added.
examples: The sequel is a *rehash* of the first film.
His speech was a *rehash* of last year's.
We don't need another *rehash* of that argument.

gloss: The act of refusing to accept someone or something.
examples: She got a *rejection* from three schools.
Fear of *rejection* kept him quiet.
The body's *rejection* of the transplant was quick.

gloss: A connection between things, or a member of your family.
examples: The price bears no *relation* to the quality.
He's a distant *relation* on my father's side.
The two events have no *relation* at all.

gloss: The physics theory linking space, time, and gravity, or the fact that something depends on the point of view.
examples: Einstein published general *relativity* in 1915.
GPS satellites have to correct for *relativity*.
The lecture ended on the *relativity* of moral standards.

gloss: A race in which team members take turns, or an electrical switch that lets one circuit control another.
examples: Our team won the four-hundred-meter *relay*.
The furnace *relay* burned out.
Ambulances ran in *relays* all night.

gloss: The quality of being connected to the matter at hand and therefore important.
examples: I don't see the *relevance* of that question.
The judge doubted the *relevance* of the emails.
The old law has lost its *relevance*.

gloss: The state of depending on someone or something.
examples: The country's *reliance* on imported oil has dropped.
Too much *reliance* on the map makes you a bad navigator.
Their *reliance* on volunteers is total.

gloss: Something that lessens pain or stress, or a baseball pitcher who comes in to replace another.
examples: Take a pain *reliever* and lie down.
The *reliever* struck out the side.
Both *relievers* warmed up in the seventh.

gloss: A chopped pickled condiment for hot dogs and sandwiches, or great enjoyment taken in something.
examples: He put mustard and *relish* on his hot dog.
She told the story with obvious *relish*.
There's a jar of *relish* in the door of the fridge.

gloss: The part that is left after the rest is taken away or used.
examples: We spent the *remainder* of the day at the beach.
Seven divided by two leaves a *remainder* of one.
The *remainder* of the money went to taxes.

gloss: A new version of a film or song that was made before.
examples: The *remake* got worse reviews than the original.
Hollywood loves a *remake*.
Two *remakes* came out the same year.

gloss: A period when the signs of a serious illness fade or disappear.
examples: Her cancer has been in *remission* for three years.
The drug pushed the disease into *remission*.
He talks about *remission*, not a cure.

gloss: Money sent to someone, especially by a worker to family in another country.
examples: *Remittances* make up a tenth of that country's economy.
He sends a *remittance* home every month.
The bank charges a fee on each *remittance*.

gloss: The act of taking something away or taking someone out of a position.
examples: Snow *removal* starts at four in the morning.
The board voted for his *removal*.
*Removal* of the old tile took two days.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A liquid or chemical made to take something off a surface.
examples: She used nail polish *remover* on the stain.
Buy a good rust *remover* for the railing.
The store carries three different *removers*.

gloss: A strong revival of interest or activity in something.
examples: The neighborhood is having a *renaissance*.
Vinyl records went through a *renaissance*.
The team's *renaissance* began with a new coach.
contrast: Capitalized, *the Renaissance* names the European period; lowercase, it means any revival.

gloss: A drawing or computer image showing how something will look, or a performance of a piece of music.
examples: The architect showed us a *rendering* of the lobby.
Her *rendering* of the aria brought the house down.
The firm sent over three *renderings*.

gloss: A particular performance or version of a song, poem, or role.
examples: His *rendition* of the anthem was slow but moving.
I like her *rendition* better than the original.
The band played two *renditions* back to back.

gloss: Someone who abandons a group, a cause, or a set of rules.
examples: A few *renegades* broke away from the party.
He built a career as a *renegade* in the industry.
The *renegade* refused every order.

gloss: A person who pays to live in or use property owned by someone else.
examples: Half the households in the city are *renters*.
The *renter* is responsible for utilities.
New rules protect *renters* from sudden increases.

gloss: An informal short form of representative, or one repetition of an exercise.
examples: A sales *rep* called about the contract.
Do ten *reps* and then rest.
Talk to your union *rep* first.

gloss: A man whose job is fixing machines or appliances.
examples: The *repairman* said the compressor was shot.
Two *repairmen* came out for the furnace.
We waited all morning for the *repairman*.
contrast: The plural is *repairmen*, not *repairmans*; *repair person* avoids naming a gender.

gloss: Payment made to make up for serious harm done, usually used in the plural.
examples: The city debated *reparations* for past housing policy.
The treaty required heavy *reparations*.
No amount of *reparation* undoes a loss like that.

gloss: The act of paying money back, or an amount paid back.
examples: Student loan *repayment* starts six months after graduation.
He missed two *repayments* in a row.
The plan stretches *repayment* over ten years.

gloss: Something that happens or is shown again just as before.
examples: Tonight's episode is a *repeat*.
Nobody wants a *repeat* of last year's flood.
The channel runs *repeats* all summer.

gloss: An indirect and usually bad result of an action, felt some time later.
examples: The decision had *repercussions* across the industry.
He never faced any *repercussions*.
One careless email had serious *repercussions*.

gloss: The act of doing or saying the same thing more than once.
examples: Learning a language takes *repetition*.
The essay suffers from *repetition*.
Endless *repetition* dulled the joke.

gloss: A person or thing that takes the place of another.
examples: They hired a *replacement* within a week.
His knee *replacement* went well.
We ordered *replacements* for the broken tiles.

gloss: The act of copying something exactly, or of repeating an experiment to check its result.
examples: DNA *replication* happens before a cell divides.
The study failed *replication* twice.
*Replication* is what separates science from one lucky finding.

gloss: A place or system where things are stored or collected, including files and code.
examples: The archive is a *repository* of family letters.
Push your changes to the shared *repository*.
Both *repositories* hold the same files.

gloss: The use of force to control people, or the pushing of feelings out of conscious thought.
examples: Years of political *repression* followed the coup.
The therapist talked about *repression* of anger.
*Repression* only made the movement grow.

gloss: A delay or temporary escape from something bad.
examples: The rain gave the firefighters a brief *reprieve*.
The governor granted a *reprieve* hours before the execution.
The factory got a one-year *reprieve*.

gloss: An act of harming someone in return for harm they caused.
examples: Workers feared *reprisal* for speaking up.
The strike was a *reprisal* for the border raid.
There were no *reprisals* after the surrender.

gloss: Criticism or blame expressed toward someone.
examples: Her record is beyond *reproach*.
There was *reproach* in his voice.
He said it without a hint of *reproach*.

gloss: The biological process of producing offspring, or a copy of a work of art.
examples: The class studied plant *reproduction*.
That painting is a *reproduction*, not the original.
The gallery sells *reproductions* in the gift shop.

gloss: An act of politely or formally asking for something.
examples: We received a *request* for more information.
The song was played at her *request*.
All *requests* go through the front desk.

gloss: A church service or a piece of music written for the dead.
examples: Mozart never finished his *requiem*.
The choir sang a *requiem* for the victims.
The article reads like a *requiem* for the old downtown.

gloss: Something that is needed or that must be done to satisfy a rule.
examples: A high school diploma is a *requirement* for the job.
She finished her language *requirement* in one year.
The building fails two safety *requirements*.

gloss: The act of selling again something you bought, or the value it keeps for that purpose.
examples: Trucks hold their *resale* value well.
The tickets were bought for *resale*.
He runs a *resale* shop on Main Street.

gloss: A supply kept back for later use, or an area of land protected for wildlife.
examples: The bank keeps cash in *reserve*.
We hiked through a nature *reserve*.
The country's oil *reserves* are shrinking.

gloss: The act of putting something back to its starting state, or a fresh start.
examples: A factory *reset* wiped the phone clean.
The two sides want a *reset* in relations.
Hold the button down for a hard *reset*.

gloss: The house or place where someone lives, or the fact of living somewhere.
examples: The fire damaged a private *residence*.
He took up *residence* in Chicago that fall.
Several *residences* were evacuated.

gloss: A period of hospital training for a new doctor, or the status of legally living in a place.
examples: She matched into a surgical *residency* in Boston.
You need one year of *residency* for in-state tuition.
The band has a weekend *residency* at that club.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A sticky substance that comes from trees, or a similar plastic-like material used in crafts and industry.
examples: Pine *resin* stuck to my hands.
She pours *resin* over her tabletops.
The kit comes with two *resins* to mix.

gloss: An electrical part that limits the flow of current in a circuit.
examples: Solder the *resistor* to the board.
The kit has fifty *resistors* in ten values.
A burned *resistor* gives off a sharp smell.
contrast: *Resistor* is the electrical part; a person who resists is a *resister*.

gloss: A deep or lasting effect on people's feelings, or the sound made when one vibration reinforces another.
examples: The speech still has *resonance* today.
The hall was built for *resonance*.
Her story had special *resonance* for me.

gloss: A supply of something useful, such as money, materials, staff, or information.
examples: The library is a great *resource* for job seekers.
The country is rich in natural *resources*.
We ran out of time and *resources*.
contrast: Americans stress the first syllable, REE-sors; British speakers say rih-ZORS.

gloss: The process of breathing, or the way cells use oxygen to release energy.
examples: The nurse recorded his *respiration* and pulse.
Plant *respiration* continues at night.
*Respiration* slows during deep sleep.

gloss: A person who answers a survey, or the party who answers a legal claim.
examples: Sixty percent of *respondents* said they would move.
Each *respondent* got the same list of questions.
The *respondent* has thirty days to reply.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A period of relaxing or sleeping, or the part of something that remains.
examples: Get some *rest* before the drive.
I'll finish the *rest* tomorrow.
The score has two whole *rests* in that measure.

gloss: The state of being unable to stay still or feel satisfied.
examples: A growing *restlessness* spread through the crowd.
His *restlessness* kept him changing jobs.
*Restlessness* at night can signal a real problem.

gloss: Self-control, or a limit placed on what someone can do.
examples: The officers showed remarkable *restraint*.
Spending *restraint* is back on the agenda.
He wrote about it with unusual *restraint*.

gloss: A rule or condition that limits what can be done.
examples: There are *restrictions* on where you can park.
The visa carries a travel *restriction*.
The city lifted its water *restrictions*.

gloss: Action taken to hurt someone because they hurt you first.
examples: The strike was framed as *retaliation*.
She feared *retaliation* from her boss.
The law protects whistleblowers from *retaliation*.

gloss: A quick, sharp reply, often an angry one.
examples: His *retort* silenced the room.
She had a *retort* ready for every question.
The *retorts* flew back and forth all evening.

gloss: A public statement taking back something said or published earlier.
examples: The paper printed a *retraction* on page two.
The journal issued a *retraction* of the study.
He demanded a full *retraction*.

gloss: A second trial of a case in court.
examples: The hung jury led to a *retrial*.
The judge ordered a *retrial* for next spring.
Both *retrials* ended in acquittals.

gloss: Severe punishment given in return for a serious wrong.
examples: He spoke of justice, not *retribution*.
The families wanted *retribution*.
Fear of *retribution* kept the witnesses quiet.

gloss: The act of getting something back or finding stored information.
examples: Data *retrieval* took the technician an hour.
*Retrieval* of the wreckage began at dawn.
Memory *retrieval* gets slower when you're tired.

gloss: A change that adds new equipment or features to an older building or machine.
examples: The school got a lighting *retrofit*.
A seismic *retrofit* costs a fortune.
Two *retrofits* cut the energy bill in half.

gloss: A look back at past events, used almost always in the phrase in retrospect.
examples: In *retrospect*, we should have left earlier.
In *retrospect* the warning signs were obvious.
*Retrospect* makes everyone a genius.

gloss: Deep respect mixed with a kind of awe.
examples: He speaks of his teacher with *reverence*.
The crowd fell into a hush of *reverence*.
There is real *reverence* for that old building.

gloss: A Christian minister, or the title used before such a minister's name.
examples: The *reverend* opened the meeting with a prayer.
She married a *reverend* from Ohio.
Two *reverends* signed the letter.
contrast: *Reverend* is the minister; *reverent* is the adjective meaning full of deep respect.

gloss: A complete change to the opposite, or the overturning of an earlier decision.
examples: The court's *reversal* surprised everyone.
That's a total *reversal* of his old position.
The team suffered a string of *reversals*.

gloss: Something given in return for good work, help, or useful information.
examples: There's a ten-thousand-dollar *reward* for the missing dog.
Hard work brings its own *rewards*.
He got a bonus as a *reward*.

gloss: A new version of a text that has been written again.
examples: The script went through four *rewrites*.
The bill needs a complete *rewrite*.
Her *rewrite* cut ten pages.
contrast: The noun is REE-ryt; the verb *rewrite* is ree-RYT, stressed on the second syllable.

gloss: The art of persuasive speaking and writing, or language that sounds impressive but may be empty.
examples: The campaign *rhetoric* got uglier every week.
She teaches *rhetoric* at the university.
Strip away the *rhetoric* and there's no plan.
contrast: The h after the r is silent: RET-uh-rik.

gloss: An older general word for pain and stiffness in the joints and muscles.
examples: Her *rheumatism* acts up in damp weather.
He blamed the *rheumatism* in his hands.
Doctors now name the exact disease instead of saying *rheumatism*.
contrast: The h is silent and the first syllable is ROO, not RYOO.

gloss: A large evergreen shrub with showy clusters of flowers.
examples: The *rhododendrons* bloom in late May.
She planted a *rhododendron* by the porch.
A row of *rhododendrons* hid the fence.

gloss: The quality of being full, deep, or abundant.
examples: The *richness* of the soil surprised the farmers.
I love the *richness* of her voice.
The *richness* of the sauce was too much for me.

gloss: The bounce of a bullet or other object off a hard surface.
examples: He was hit by a *ricochet*.
The puck went in on a *ricochet*.
*Ricochets* make a shooting range dangerous.
contrast: The final t is silent: RIK-uh-shay.

gloss: Someone riding a horse, bike, or vehicle, or an extra clause attached to a bill or policy.
examples: The *rider* fell but got right back on.
Bus *riders* pay two dollars.
A *rider* on the spending bill funded the bridge.

gloss: Unkind laughter or comments meant to make someone look foolish.
examples: The proposal drew *ridicule* online.
He faced years of *ridicule* over that haircut.
Public *ridicule* is a poor teacher.

gloss: A serious break in a relationship, or a crack or split in rock or ice.
examples: A *rift* opened between the two brothers.
The party is trying to heal the *rift*.
A deep *rift* runs across the glacier.

gloss: A large piece of equipment such as a drilling platform, or a big truck.
examples: The *rig* pumps oil around the clock.
He drove an eighteen-wheeler and kept his *rig* spotless.
They set up a lighting *rig* over the stage.

gloss: Short, wide, ridged tubes of pasta.
examples: She baked *rigatoni* with sausage and cheese.
A pound of *rigatoni* feeds four people.
The *rigatoni* holds the sauce better than spaghetti.

gloss: The quality of being stiff, or of refusing to change or bend.
examples: The frame's *rigidity* keeps the wheels aligned.
His *rigidity* about the rules cost him friends.
There's a *rigidity* to the schedule that nobody likes.

gloss: The person who leads others in trouble or crime.
examples: Police identified the *ringleader* of the theft ring.
He was the *ringleader* of every prank in school.
Two *ringleaders* were charged.

gloss: A person taking part in violent public disorder.
examples: *Rioters* smashed the storefront windows.
A *rioter* was arrested two blocks away.
Police pushed the *rioters* back.

gloss: A torn place in cloth, paper, or similar material.
examples: There's a *rip* in the knee of my jeans.
He found a small *rip* in the tent.
The *rips* got worse with every wash.

gloss: An increase in amount, level, or importance.
examples: The *rise* in rents pushed families out.
We watched the *rise* of a whole new industry.
There have been three price *rises* this year.
contrast: In the US a pay increase is a *raise*; British speakers call that a *rise*.

gloss: An Italian dish of rice cooked slowly in broth until it turns creamy.
examples: He made mushroom *risotto* for dinner.
Good *risotto* needs constant stirring.
Their two *risottos* are the best things on the menu.

gloss: The ground at the bottom of a river.
examples: The drought left the *riverbed* cracked and dry.
We hiked along the dry *riverbed*.
Gravel from the *riverbed* went into the road.

gloss: Animals killed by passing vehicles on a road.
examples: Vultures were picking at *roadkill* on the shoulder.
We passed a lot of *roadkill* on that stretch.
The team lost so badly they looked like *roadkill*.

gloss: A fast-running desert bird of the American Southwest.
examples: A *roadrunner* darted across the highway.
*Roadrunners* eat lizards and even small snakes.
We saw a *roadrunner* just outside Tucson.

gloss: A loud, deep sound made by an animal, a crowd, or an engine.
examples: The lion's *roar* carried across the valley.
A *roar* went up from the stands.
You could hear the *roar* of the surf from the porch.

gloss: A dishonest or unpredictable person who acts outside the rules.
examples: A few *rogues* gave the whole trade a bad name.
The film's hero is a lovable *rogue*.
One *rogue* trader lost the bank millions.
contrast: *Rogue* rhymes with *vogue*; do not confuse it with *rouge*, the makeup.

gloss: A reduction or cancellation of something that was put in place earlier.
examples: The agency announced a *rollback* of the emissions rule.
Shoppers welcomed the price *rollback*.
Several *rollbacks* are tied up in court.

gloss: A love relationship, a story about love, or the exciting feeling something gives.
examples: Their office *romance* lasted about two months.
She reads a *romance* every week.
There's a certain *romance* to train travel.

gloss: A worker who builds and repairs roofs.
examples: The *roofer* found three cracked shingles.
We got bids from four *roofers*.
A good *roofer* is booked months out.

gloss: The material a roof is made of, or the work of putting a roof on.
examples: Metal *roofing* lasts about fifty years.
He's been in *roofing* since high school.
We ordered enough *roofing* for the shed.

gloss: The chess piece shaped like a castle tower, or a black European bird of the crow family.
examples: She castled and slid her *rook* to the open file.
Both *rooks* were traded off early.
A flock of *rooks* settled on the plowed field.

gloss: A rose flower that has not opened yet.
examples: He handed her a single *rosebud*.
The *rosebuds* opened after two warm days.
A *rosebud* was pinned to his lapel.

gloss: A dark, hard tropical wood used for furniture and musical instruments.
examples: The guitar has a *rosewood* fingerboard.
That table is solid *rosewood*.
*Rosewood* is now heavily restricted in trade.

gloss: Turning around a center point, or a regular taking of turns.
examples: The earth's *rotation* takes about twenty-four hours.
Nurses work on a three-shift *rotation*.
Crop *rotation* keeps the soil healthy.

gloss: Learning by pure repetition, without understanding.
examples: We learned the times tables by *rote*.
*Rote* memorization won't help on this exam.
He recites the whole thing by *rote* every morning.
contrast: *Rote* sounds exactly like *wrote*, the past tense of *write*.

gloss: A rotating spit for roasting meat, or meat cooked on one.
examples: Pick up a *rotisserie* chicken on the way home.
The deli has a *rotisserie* right behind the counter.
Both *rotisseries* were running at full speed.

gloss: The turning part of a machine, such as a helicopter's blades or a brake disc.
examples: The helicopter's *rotor* kicked up a wall of dust.
The mechanic replaced the front *rotors*.
A bent *rotor* makes the brakes shudder.

gloss: A large, powerful black-and-tan breed of guard dog.
examples: Their *rottweiler* barks at every delivery truck.
*Rottweilers* need firm, early training.
A *rottweiler* met us at the gate.

gloss: Red makeup put on the cheeks.
examples: She wore a little *rouge* and nothing else.
The actor's *rouge* looked heavy under the lights.
Most Americans now say blush instead of *rouge*.
contrast: *Rouge* ends in the ZH sound, like the middle of *measure* — do not confuse it with *rogue*.

gloss: The fibrous part of food that helps digestion.
examples: Beans and greens give you plenty of *roughage*.
The diet is short on *roughage*.
Doctors used to say *roughage*; now they say fiber.
contrast: The gh sounds like f: RUF-ij.

gloss: The quality of having an uneven surface, or of being harsh in manner.
examples: You can feel the *roughness* of the unfinished wood.
There was a *roughness* in his voice.
Sanding took the *roughness* off the edge.

gloss: A casino game in which players bet on where a ball will land on a spinning wheel.
examples: He lost fifty dollars at *roulette*.
The *roulette* wheel spun for what felt like a minute.
Crossing that street is like Russian *roulette*.
